title: The Consequences of More Words But Less Reading
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that the explosion of text people encounter daily through smartphones - captions, notifications, headlines, messages - has not made people more literate, because most of that exposure is processed through skimming rather than genuine reading. It draws a sharp distinction between reading, which builds a full mental picture and requires rereading when something doesn't add up, and skimming, which processes fragments for identification and, according to cited research, diminishes retention and crowds out the inference, empathy, and perspective-taking that deep reading cultivates. Rather than recommending less phone use, the piece's prescribed fix is developing a 'bi-literate' brain that deliberately practices both fast scanning and slow, sustained reading, much as an athlete cross-trains different muscle groups. It closes with a practical leadership habit: building a shared reading set into team discussions as preparation for debate, and holding that requirement even against pushback, on the argument that insisting on reading is itself what makes a team better at thinking.
points: The piece distinguishes true reading — building a mental picture, filling in implications, rereading until it coheres — from skimming, which processes fragments for identification rather than comprehension.
It cites research that deep reading underlies core intellectual and emotional capacities (reasoning, inference, empathy, perspective-taking) that skimming does not develop or sustain.
Rather than recommending less screen time, the piece's prescribed solution is building a 'bi-literate' brain that deliberately cross-trains both fast scanning and slow, print-style deep reading.
The concrete leadership practice recommended is requiring a shared reading set ahead of team discussions and holding the line on it even when people push back.
quotes: Practically speaking, reading is the act of turning symbols on a page or screen into meaning in your head. And it happens in layers.

Glancing at messages, posts, and notifications is a very different activity from sustained reading for comprehension and reflection. For many people, thoughtful reading has been replaced by the activity of skimming.
Research is clear that because skimming encourages people to jump from spot to spot and focus on keywords, it diminishes their ability to absorb and retain what's been written.

Many academics have argued that deep reading underlies our most important intellectual and emotional capacities, such as reasoning, inference, empathy, insight, perspective-taking, and critical analysis.

The most agreed-upon solution isn't to limit access to smartphones or to encourage people to skim less digitally, but rather to develop a "bi-literate" brain that can both scan fast and go deep with print-style reading.

Good leaders haven't given up on requiring team members to read. They build into team discussions a common reading set for everyone to digest and contemplate as preparation for robust debate on a topic, issue, or decision.
If people complain, they smile and insist that reading is a requisite skill too important to ignore. Directly and indirectly, their insistence makes people better thinkers.
